section: Prerequisites / You will learn / Why this matters
question: In supervised fine-tuning of a language model, what is a chat template?
options: A fixed, deterministic rule that flattens a list of role-tagged messages into one delimited token string
A learned embedding layer that converts each conversation role into a separate vector before the first attention block
A sampling strategy that decides how many tokens the assistant may generate in each turn
A dataset filter that removes low-quality conversations before fine-tuning begins
explanation: A chat template is the exact, deterministic serialization rule that turns a list of role-tagged messages into a single string with delimiter tokens. It is not learned and has no parameters; it is the interface between a conversation and a sequence of token ids. Because it is fixed, the model can learn where the assistant turn begins and when to stop.

section: Prerequisites / You will learn / Why this matters
question: Which post-training stages operate on chat-formatted data?
options: Only SFT; reward modeling and DPO operate on raw pretraining documents
Only RLHF, because it is the only stage that samples from the model
None of them; chat formatting is applied only at inference time
SFT, reward modeling, RLHF and DPO all operate on chat-formatted data
explanation: Everything after pretraining — SFT, reward modeling, RLHF, DPO — consumes chat-formatted data. That is why the chat template is the foundational interface of post-training. Formatting applied only at inference would mismatch the training distribution.

section: Prerequisites / You will learn / Why this matters
question: What is the typical symptom when the chat template used at inference is inconsistent with the one used in fine-tuning?
options: The tokenizer raises an exception, because the new delimiters are missing from its vocabulary
The loss becomes NaN on the first inference step, so generation outputs only padding tokens afterwards
The model silently degrades, often never seeing the stop delimiter it learned and rambling on
The model refuses to answer and returns an empty string for every prompt it is given
explanation: Template mismatch does not crash anything; the model is simply off-distribution. A typical outcome is that it never sees or emits the delimiter it was trained to stop on, so it keeps generating. The failure is silent, which makes it dangerous.

question: What was the only training objective of a pretrained GPT-2-style model?
options: Predict a helpful response to a user request given a system prompt
Predict the next token given the tokens so far, via cross-entropy loss
Classify whether each document is high- or low-quality web text
Reconstruct randomly masked tokens anywhere in the sequence
explanation: Pretraining optimizes next-token cross-entropy: given the prefix, predict the next token. Trained on a large text pile, the model becomes very good at continuing text. It never sees an objective about answering requests, and GPT-style models are causal, not masked-token models.

question: Why might a purely pretrained model continue the prompt 'Write a haiku about the sea.' with 'Write a haiku about the mountains.'?
options: Because the model's context window is too short to hold a full haiku, so it restarts the prompt from scratch
Because in web text, a line that looks like a writing prompt is most often followed by another prompt in a list
Because pretraining loss was computed only on the prompt tokens, never on the answers that follow them in web text
Because the model has a bug in its sampling loop that copies the input back to the output with one word changed
explanation: The pretrained model models text continuation. In its corpus, lines like 'Write a haiku about X' usually appear in lists of writing prompts, so the most probable continuation is another prompt. The model is doing its job perfectly; its job just is not following instructions.

question: What does a pretrained language model fundamentally model, as opposed to an instruction-tuned one?
options: What tokens plausibly come next in a document like the given text
What answer best fulfils the user's request
Which of several candidate responses a human would prefer
Which role (system, user, or assistant) is speaking at each position
explanation: A pretrained LM models text continuation — what plausibly comes next in a document like this one. Nothing in pretraining tells it a prompt is a request to fulfil. Preferences are learned later (reward modeling/DPO), and roles only exist once chat templates are introduced in SFT.

question: How does supervised fine-tuning (SFT) teach a pretrained model to follow instructions?
options: By adding a new classification head that detects instructions in the prompt
By training a reward model and then optimizing against it with PPO
By freezing the model and only editing its tokenizer vocabulary
By continuing training on curated (prompt, ideal response) pairs
explanation: SFT continues training on demonstrations: curated pairs of a prompt and the ideal response. After enough of these, the plausible continuation of a request becomes a helpful answer. Reward models and PPO belong to RLHF, a later stage.

section: 1. Intuition: SFT is just more next-token training, on different data
question: Relative to pretraining, what does SFT change about the model architecture and loss function?
options: It adds a response head and switches to a ranking loss
It keeps the architecture but replaces cross-entropy with a mean-squared error
Neither; it uses the same architecture and the same next-token cross-entropy
It changes the architecture to an encoder-decoder but keeps cross-entropy
explanation: SFT is just more next-token training: same architecture, same cross-entropy loss. What changes is the data (demonstrations of desired behavior) and where the loss is applied (response tokens only). That simplicity is why SFT is the cheapest post-training step.

section: 1. Intuition: SFT is just more next-token training, on different data
question: Which two things change when moving from pretraining to SFT?
options: The optimizer (SGD instead of AdamW) and the tokenizer (word-level instead of byte-level BPE)
The model depth (extra layers for the response) and the attention mechanism (bidirectional)
The training data (demonstrations) and which positions the loss is applied to (response only)
The learning-rate schedule (constant instead of cosine) and the vocabulary size (chat tokens only)
explanation: SFT swaps raw documents for demonstrations of the target behavior, and it scores only the response tokens, not the prompt. Architecture, optimizer family, and tokenizer are unchanged. These two changes are what make the continuation of a request become a helpful answer.

section: 1. Intuition: SFT is just more next-token training, on different data
question: In the post-training pipeline, what is SFT shaping, given what pretraining already installed?
options: Knowledge, replacing the behavior pretraining installed
Behavior, on top of the knowledge pretraining already installed
Tokenization, on top of the embeddings pretraining installed
Model capacity, by adding parameters that pretraining did not have
explanation: Post-training (SFT, reward modeling, RLHF/DPO) is about shaping behavior on top of the knowledge that pretraining already put in the weights. SFT is the first and cheapest of these steps. It does not add capacity or replace knowledge.

section: 1. Intuition: SFT is just more next-token training, on different data
question: Which is the order of the standard post-training pipeline?
options: SFT, then reward model, then RLHF/DPO
Reward model, then SFT, then pretraining
RLHF, then SFT, then reward model
DPO, then pretraining, then SFT
explanation: The standard pipeline runs SFT first (cheapest, imitation of demonstrations), then trains a reward model, then optimizes behavior with RLHF or DPO. Pretraining comes before all of them. SFT is described as the first and cheapest step.

question: What are the three fields of the classic FLAN/Alpaca instruction-tuning example?
options: system, user, assistant
question, context, and label
prompt, chosen, rejected
instruction, input, output
explanation: The classic shape is (instruction, [input], output): what to do, optionally what to do it to, and the demonstrated ideal response. 'system/user/assistant' are chat roles, and 'prompt/chosen/rejected' is the preference-data format used later for reward modeling and DPO.

question: In an (instruction, [input], output) triple, which field is optional?
options: instruction
output
none; all three are always required
input
explanation: The input is optional: some instructions are self-contained, such as 'Write a haiku about the sea.' The instruction and output are always needed, since the output is what the model is trained to produce.

question: In an instruction triple, which fields together form the prompt, and which is the training target?
options: Instruction alone is the prompt; input plus output together form the target the model is trained on
Input alone is the prompt; instruction plus output together form the target the model must produce
Instruction plus input form the prompt; output is what the model is trained to produce
All three fields are concatenated, and every token of all three is scored equally as the target
explanation: The instruction and optional input together form the prompt, and the output is the demonstrated response the model learns to produce. Scoring the prompt as a target would teach the model to generate instructions, which SFT avoids by masking.

question: For the triple instruction='Translate the sentence to French.', input='The cat sat on the mat.', what role does 'Le chat s'est assis sur le tapis.' play?
options: The input: the data that the instruction acts on
The output: the demonstrated ideal response
The system message: persistent behavior
The instruction: what to do
explanation: The French sentence is the output field — the demonstrated ideal response. The English sentence is the input (the thing to act on) and 'Translate the sentence to French.' is the instruction. The triple format has no system field.

question: How was the FLAN instruction dataset (Wei et al. 2021) built?
options: By rewriting existing NLP datasets as natural-language instructions using many phrasing templates
By having a strong LM generate new instruction triples from a handful of human-written seed examples
By collecting human preference rankings between pairs of model responses to the same instruction
By scraping question-answer forums and keeping only the accepted or most upvoted answer per thread
explanation: FLAN took existing NLP datasets (translation, summarization, QA, sentiment, ...) and rephrased each as natural-language instructions with many templates. Generating triples from seeds with an LM is Self-Instruct; preference rankings are reward-modeling data.

question: What generalization result motivates FLAN-style instruction tuning?
options: Fine-tuning on a mixture of instruction-phrased tasks lets the model follow unseen instructions zero-shot
Fine-tuning on one task makes the model better only at that exact task, so each task needs its own run
Fine-tuning on instructions removes the need for pretraining, since instructions carry the needed knowledge
Fine-tuning on instructions makes the model's tokenizer more compact, so unseen prompts use fewer tokens
explanation: FLAN showed that training on a mixture of many tasks phrased as instructions makes the model generalize to instructions it has never seen, zero-shot. It builds on pretraining rather than replacing it, and has nothing to do with tokenizer size.

question: How does Self-Instruct (Wang et al. 2022) create instruction data?
options: Rewrite existing labelled NLP datasets into instruction form with many phrasing templates, then train on the whole mixture
Hire annotators to write every instruction-response pair by hand, then have a second annotator verify each one
Sample many responses from the model and keep those a learned reward model scores highest, then train on them
Seed a few human-written examples, have a strong LM generate many more triples, filter for quality, and train on them
explanation: Self-Instruct bootstraps: start from a small set of human seeds, have a strong LM generate many (instruction, input, output) triples, filter for quality, and fine-tune on the result. This avoids hand-writing every example. Template rewriting of existing datasets is FLAN's approach.

question: Which well-known instruction dataset was built with the Self-Instruct recipe?
options: FLAN
The GPT-2 WebText corpus
Alpaca
Common Crawl
explanation: Alpaca used the Self-Instruct recipe: LM-generated instruction triples bootstrapped from seeds. FLAN rewrote existing NLP datasets, and WebText/Common Crawl are pretraining corpora, not instruction data.

question: When reading the FLAN and Self-Instruct papers for SFT, which parts are recommended to read closely versus skip?
options: Read the per-task appendices closely for the templates; skip the data-construction sections on a first pass
Read the data-construction sections closely; skip the long per-task appendices on a first pass
Read only the abstracts and related-work sections, then go straight to the released datasets and code
Skip both papers entirely on a first pass; they are optional background for anyone doing SFT in practice
explanation: Both are core Module 14 readings. The data-construction sections carry the key ideas — instructions as a training distribution and how to generate it cheaply — while the long per-task appendices can be skipped at first.

question: How can a single-turn (instruction, input, output) triple be represented as a chat?
options: As a three-message chat: a system message (instruction), a user message (input), an assistant message (output)
As a two-message chat: a user message (instruction + input) and an assistant message (output)
As a single user message containing all three fields, with the output kept as an unscored suffix
As a single assistant message containing all three fields, so every token is trained as a response
explanation: A single-turn triple is just a user message holding the instruction and input, followed by an assistant message holding the output. A system message is a separate, optional element that sets persistent behavior; it is not where the instruction goes.

question: In multi-turn chat data, what is the purpose of a system message?
options: To set persistent behavior for the conversation, such as 'You are a terse assistant.'
To mark the end of every turn, so the model knows when it should stop generating
To hold the model's demonstrated responses, which are the tokens scored in training
To store the user's previous conversation history once it no longer fits in context
explanation: The system message sets persistent behavior that applies across the conversation, e.g. 'You are a terse assistant.' Ending turns is the job of the end delimiter, and responses live in assistant messages. The general object to format is therefore a list of role-tagged messages.

question: Why is a chat template needed at all before a conversation can be fed to a language model?
options: Because the model needs each role encoded as a separate input tensor alongside the token ids
Because tokenizers cannot handle newline characters, so turns must be joined with special tokens
Because attention requires every turn to be padded to the same length before it can be batched
Because the model consumes a flat sequence of token ids, not a list of role-tagged dicts
explanation: The model eats one flat sequence of token ids. A list of message dicts must therefore be serialized into one string, with delimiters marking turn boundaries and roles. There is no separate role tensor; the role information lives in the delimiter tokens.

question: In a chat template, what is the load-bearing role of the special delimiter tokens?
options: They compress the conversation so that long multi-turn chats fit inside the context window
They tell the tokenizer which language each turn is written in, so it picks the right merges
They are the only signal the model has for a new turn, who is speaking, and when the turn is over
They carry the positional encoding for each turn, so that the model can tell how far back each turn is
explanation: Delimiters are the only signal for 'a new turn started', 'this is the assistant speaking', and crucially 'the turn is over, stop generating'. Without them the model could not distinguish roles or learn to stop. They do not compress text or carry positions.

question: In the course's chat template, which four delimiter tokens are used?
options: <|im_start|>, <|im_end|>, [INST] and [/INST]
<bos>, <eos>, <pad> and <unk>
<|system|>, <|user|>, <|assistant|> and <|end|>
<|system|>, <|user|>, <|assistant|> and <|pad|>, with <|pad|> closing turns
explanation: The template uses three role headers (<|system|>, <|user|>, <|assistant|>) that open a turn and one end-of-turn token <|end|> that closes it. <|im_start|>/<|im_end|> and [INST]/[/INST] are other model families' delimiters.

question: In the course's chat template, how is one message rendered?
options: The content first, then the role header after it, then a newline
Role header, a newline, the content, then <|end|> and a newline
Role header, then the content on the same line, a newline, and no end token
<|end|> first to close the previous turn, then the role header, the content, a newline
explanation: Each message becomes: its role header, a newline, its content, then <|end|> and a newline. Messages are concatenated. For example: '<|user|>\nCapital of France?<|end|>\n'.

question: Why must chat delimiter tokens like <|end|> be treated as atomic by the tokenizer?
options: So each is exactly one id and is never split into pieces like '<', '|', 'end'
So they are always mapped to the padding id and ignored by attention and the loss
So they can be merged with neighbouring words by BPE to save tokens in long chats
So the model can predict them character by character and learn their exact spelling
explanation: Delimiters must be one id each, never split into '<', '|', 'system', etc. Splitting would blur the boundary the model must learn and make it context-dependent. This is the special-token machinery of a production tokenizer.

question: Why must chat delimiter tokens be reserved in the tokenizer?
options: So they are excluded from the model's output vocabulary and can never be sampled
So they do not count toward the context length when long chats are truncated
So they are always placed at the start of the sequence, before any user text
So ordinary user text cannot forge them and fake a turn boundary
explanation: Reserving delimiters means ordinary text cannot produce their ids, so a user typing the literal string '<|end|>' cannot forge a turn boundary — otherwise it is a prompt-injection vector. The model still outputs them (it must emit <|end|> to stop).

question: The course's from-scratch BPETokenizer does not reserve chat delimiters. How does the code keep turn boundaries exact anyway?
options: It replaces each delimiter with a single unused byte before encoding, then maps the byte back after decoding
It trains the BPE tokenizer on a corpus containing many delimiters, so they are learned as single merges
It strips all delimiters out before encoding and inserts them back into the token ids after decoding
It encodes each segment (header, content, closer) separately, so no BPE merge crosses a boundary
explanation: render_with_response_mask encodes segment by segment — role header, content, closer — so merges never span a boundary and the mask stays exact. A production tokenizer instead adds each delimiter to the vocabulary as a single id.

question: After SFT with a consistent chat template, what two behaviors has the model learned?
options: After '<|user|>\n' produce a likely user question, and after <|end|> produce a fresh system message
After '<|system|>\n' produce a helpful response, and never emit <|end|> so the reply is not cut short
After '<|assistant|>\n' produce a helpful response, and when finished emit <|end|> and stop
After any delimiter produce padding tokens until the context fills, and then emit a single <|end|>
explanation: The template is a contract learned during SFT: after the assistant header, generate a helpful response; when done, emit <|end|> and stop. This contract only holds if inference uses the same format.

question: What is the 'generation prompt' in chat-template inference?
options: A special system message appended at the end that tells the model to be helpful and to answer the last user turn
The conversation rendered through a bare '<|assistant|>\n' with no content, so the model generates the reply
The full conversation including the assistant answer, rendered once as a reference that sampling is scored against
A random prefix sampled from earlier assistant turns and prepended to the prompt to diversify the model's responses
explanation: At inference you render the conversation up to and including a bare assistant header, then call generate. The model fills in the response and emits <|end|>, at which point decoding stops. Including the answer would only be done for training data.

question: What is the most common bug when a model trained with <|end|> as the stop signal is deployed?
options: The decode loop does not treat <|end|> as a stop, so the model runs to the token limit
The model refuses to emit any tokens after the assistant header and returns empty
The model emits <|end|> as its very first token every time, so replies are empty
The tokenizer crashes on <|end|> at decode time because the token id is unknown
explanation: If train-time and inference-time formatting disagree, the model is off-distribution; the most common symptom is that it never stops. If you forget to sample until <|end|> and treat it as the end, generation continues to max tokens every time.

question: Which of these train/inference differences would put an SFT model off-distribution?
options: Any of: a missing newline, a different role header, or no end token
Only using a different random seed at inference than in training
Only using a larger batch size at inference than during training
Only running inference on a different GPU model than training
explanation: The model learned the exact template string. A missing newline, a different header, or a missing end token all change the token sequence it conditions on, so the model is off-distribution. Seeds, batch sizes, or hardware do not change the format.

question: In the course's llmre.sft.chat_template module, what does render_chat(messages[:2], add_generation_prompt=True) produce for a system and a user message?
options: The rendered system and user turns followed by a closing '<|end|>' only
Only the user turn with a bare '<|assistant|>\n', the system turn dropped
The full three-turn chat, including the assistant's answer and its <|end|>
The rendered system and user turns followed by a bare '<|assistant|>\n'
explanation: With add_generation_prompt=True, render_chat renders the given messages and appends the assistant header with no content, ready for generation. Without it, it renders exactly the messages given, which for training includes assistant content.

question: What does render_with_response_mask(messages, encode) return?
options: A torch.long tensor of token ids and a causal attention mask of shape (T, T) over all turns
A rendered string and the character index at which the first assistant turn's content starts
A list of token ids and an equal-length mask with 1 exactly on assistant-response tokens
A list of token ids and a list of role names, one per message, used to weight the loss by role
explanation: It returns input_ids and response_mask, two equal-length lists; response_mask[i] == 1 iff token i belongs to an assistant response. That mask is what the next step (loss masking) uses to build labels.

question: In render_with_response_mask, which tokens are marked as response (mask = 1)?
options: The assistant's content only, excluding <|end|>
The assistant's content and its <|end|> closer
The <|assistant|> header and the assistant's content
All tokens of every turn, including system and user
explanation: Assistant content plus its <|end|> closer are marked response; system text, user text, and all role headers (including <|assistant|>) are prompt. Including the closer is deliberate: it is how the model learns to emit the stop token.

question: Why does the chat-template code deliberately mark the assistant's <|end|> closer as a response token?
options: So the closer is excluded from attention at training time and never seen
So the loss trains the model to emit the stop token at the end of its turn
So the closer is not counted toward the sequence length when packing
So the model learns to predict the next user turn after its own reply
explanation: If <|end|> were masked as prompt, the model would never be trained to produce it and would not learn to stop. Marking it as response makes emitting the stop token part of the learned behavior.

question: How does render_with_response_mask build its outputs internally?
options: It walks (text, is_response) segments, encodes each independently, and extends the ids and a repeated 0/1 flag
It renders the full string once, encodes it, then searches for the assistant header to set the mask
It encodes each character separately and marks characters after '<|assistant|>' as response
It runs the model over the rendered string and marks the tokens it predicts with high confidence as the response tokens
explanation: The function iterates over segments (header, content, closer) tagged with is_response, encodes each segment, appends its ids, and appends [1 if is_resp else 0] * len(seg_ids) to the mask. Encoding per segment keeps boundaries exact with a BPE that does not reserve delimiters.

question: What are the types returned by render_with_response_mask in the course's chat-template module?
options: Two torch.long tensors already on the training device
A torch.bool tensor and a torch.float tensor
A rendered string and a numpy int32 array of mask flags
Two equal-length Python list[int]; no tensors yet
explanation: There are no tensors in the chat-template module: messages is list[dict[str, str]], render_chat returns str, and render_with_response_mask returns two equal-length lists of Python ints. They become a torch.long tensor only later, when labels are built and batches are moved to the device.

question: In HuggingFace, what is tokenizer.apply_chat_template(messages, add_generation_prompt=...) equivalent to?
options: A learned model that rewrites the message list into a better-performing prompt, with a switch for adding few-shot examples
A function that trains the tokenizer's merges on chat data so delimiters become single tokens, run once per model
The same job as render_chat: a deterministic message-list to delimited-string rule, with a generation-prompt switch
A function that computes only the response mask for the SFT loss, returning a 0/1 list aligned with the token ids
explanation: apply_chat_template does exactly what render_chat does; the template itself is a Jinja string shipped with each chat model. Different families use different delimiters (<|im_start|>/<|im_end|>, [INST]/[/INST]), but the job is the same.

question: In HuggingFace chat models, where is the chat template itself stored?
options: As hard-coded Python inside the Transformers library, identical for all models
As learned weights inside the model's first layer
As a Jinja template string shipped with each chat model's tokenizer
As a separate fine-tuned adapter loaded at inference
explanation: Each chat model ships its own Jinja template string. That is why different families have different delimiters, and why you must use the right model's template. It is not learned and not shared across all models.

question: What goes wrong if you format SFT data for model A using model B's chat delimiters?
options: Nothing; delimiters are interchangeable across model families, since any string can mark a turn
The delimiters are not in either vocabulary as intended, so turn boundaries become gibberish
The model trains faster, because seeing more distinct delimiter tokens gives it a richer turn signal
The tokenizer automatically converts B's delimiters into A's, so the rendered data is identical anyway
explanation: Each family's delimiters are specific to its tokenizer. Using another model's delimiters means they do not exist as the intended single ids, so the turn structure the model must learn is garbled. There is no automatic conversion.

question: What can happen if you forget add_generation_prompt at inference?
options: Without the trailing '<|assistant|>\n' the model is not cued that it is its turn and may continue the user's text
The model emits <|end|> as its first token, because the last thing in context is a closed user turn, and returns nothing
The tokenizer throws an error about a missing assistant role, since every rendered chat must end with an assistant turn
The model still answers correctly but twice as slowly, because it first regenerates the missing header token by token
explanation: The trailing assistant header is the cue that the assistant should speak. Without it, the prompt ends after the user's <|end|>, and the model may continue in the wrong role, such as writing more of the user's message.

question: What is the symptom of a decode loop that ignores <|end|>?
options: No answer at all, only an empty string returned
An answer in the wrong language for the prompt
A tokenizer error raised at the end of generation
A correct answer followed by hallucinated extra turns
explanation: The model dutifully emits the stop token, but if the loop ignores it, sampling continues and the model starts inventing new turns. You get a correct answer followed by hallucinated follow-up turns.

question: Why must prompt tokens be masked out of the SFT loss?
options: Otherwise the tokenizer cannot encode the prompt tokens
Otherwise attention cannot see the prompt during training
Otherwise the context window overflows on long prompts
Otherwise you teach the model to generate user turns
explanation: If prompt tokens are scored, the model is trained to predict user and system text, i.e. to generate user turns. Masking only removes them from the loss; the model still attends to them as context.

question: After SFT on data rendered with <|end|> after every turn, a model answers correctly but then invents a follow-up question and answers it until the length limit. Where is the most likely bug?
options: In training: the rendered data never actually contained the <|end|> token
In the tokenizer: <|end|> is split into several ordinary tokens at decode time
In inference: the generation loop does not stop when <|end|> is sampled
In the optimizer: the learning rate was too high, so the model overfit to long replies
explanation: The training data included <|end|>, so the model did learn to emit it. The generation loop is not treating <|end|> as a stop and keeps sampling for max_new_tokens, so a hallucinated new turn begins. Fix: stop as soon as the sampled token is the <|end|> id or truncate at the first <|end|>.

question: When debugging a fine-tuned chat model that rambles, which observation would point to a training-formatting bug rather than an inference bug?
options: The model emits <|end|> and then keeps generating past it
The model never emits <|end|> at all
The model stops correctly when <|end|> is passed as a stop token
The model answers correctly before it starts rambling on
explanation: If the model emits <|end|> and keeps going, the inference loop ignores the stop token. If the model never emits <|end|>, it never learned to, which points to training formatting (e.g. the closer was missing or masked out).

question: What does SFT change so that the continuation of 'Write a haiku about the sea.' becomes a haiku?
options: The training distribution, so that the continuation of a request is a helpful answer
The model architecture, by adding an instruction-detection module before the first block
The sampling temperature, so that continuing with another prompt becomes less likely
The tokenizer, so that lists of writing prompts are split into different token sequences
explanation: The pretrained model continues a writing prompt with another prompt because that is common in its data. SFT changes the training distribution so that what follows a request is a helpful answer. Architecture and tokenizer are unchanged.

question: When should add_generation_prompt=True be used?
options: At inference, to render the conversation so far before generating; not when formatting training data
When formatting training data, so that the model learns to produce the assistant header on its own
Only when the conversation has a system message, to separate it from the first user turn
Always, for both training and inference, so that the rendered format is identical in the two settings
explanation: It appends an empty assistant header to cue the model's turn, which is only needed at inference. Training data already contains the assistant content after the header, so adding an extra empty header would corrupt it.
